name: Business Strategy & Writing
description: Combines strategic business thinking with professional writing — corporate strategy frameworks, competitive analysis, strategic planning documents, business cases, and writing that drives decisions.

modules.title: What Is Strategy?
modules.objectives: Distinguish strategy from tactics; identify the three levels of strategy (corporate, business, functional); articulate strategic intent and why it matters. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — strategic management and strategic intent
modules.videoNote: Harvard Business Review — “A Plan Is Not a Strategy,” on choices and coherent strategic logic
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — strategic management and strategic intent — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Write a 350-word strategy memo for the included company Northstar E-Bikes, which serves urban commuters, has limited capital, and promises reliable repairable bikes. State one three-year strategic intent and distinguish one corporate-level, one business-level, and one functional-level choice. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: a strategy-versus-tactics table, three aligned choices, two facts from the case, and one tradeoff the company must accept. Evaluation: alignment across levels (45%), use of case evidence and tradeoffs (35%), and concise professional writing (20%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion or method with cited case facts, calculations, or course rules.

modules.title: External Analysis
modules.objectives: Apply the PESTLE framework to map macro-environmental forces; use Porter's Five Forces to assess industry attractiveness; identify key opportunities and threats.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — external environment and Porter’s Five Forces
modules.videoNote: Harvard Business Review — “The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy”
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — external environment and Porter’s Five Forces — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Analyze this included Northstar market evidence: city e-bike rebates are rising; interest rates are high; two global brands cut prices; battery rules may tighten; suppliers are concentrated; substitutes include transit and scooters; customers can compare prices instantly. Build a PESTLE and Five Forces analysis. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: all six PESTLE categories, all five forces with strength ratings, three opportunities, three threats, and a recommendation supported by at least four supplied facts. Evaluation: framework accuracy (40%), evidence-based ratings (40%), and decision clarity (20%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion or method with cited case facts, calculations, or course rules.

modules.title: Internal Analysis
modules.objectives: Conduct a deep SWOT analysis; apply the resource-based view to identify core competencies; map a company's value chain to find areas of advantage.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — SWOT, internal evidence, and analytical limits
modules.videoNote: Parr and Associates — “How to SWOT analysis,” a concise framework demonstration
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — SWOT, internal evidence, and analytical limits — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Use this included Northstar evidence: a patented repairable frame, 78% repeat-service rate, one small assembly site, no mobile app, experienced technicians, $400,000 cash, and a supplier-controlled battery. Build SWOT, VRIO, and value-chain analyses. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: four SWOT quadrants, a VRIO table for three resources, two value-chain strengths or gaps, and one priority capability investment. Evaluation: correct internal/external classification (35%), VRIO/value-chain reasoning (45%), and supported priority (20%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion or method with cited case facts, calculations, or course rules.

modules.title: Competitive Advantage
modules.objectives: Define competitive advantage; compare cost leadership, differentiation, and focus strategies; explain Blue Ocean Strategy and how it differs from competing in existing market space.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — generic strategies and competitive advantage
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson and teacher-reviewed examples for this topic.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — generic strategies and competitive advantage — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Compare Northstar with the included rival FlashRide: FlashRide prices 20% lower, outsources repairs, and sells through mass retailers; Northstar offers modular parts, local service, and a two-year repair promise. Recommend cost leadership, differentiation, focus, or a defensible combination. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: a competitor table, evidence for each firm’s current positioning, one Blue Ocean eliminate-reduce-raise-create grid, and a 250-word recommendation with a stated risk. Evaluation: accurate strategy concepts (40%), evidence and tradeoff analysis (40%), and persuasive writing (20%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion or method with cited case facts, calculations, or course rules.

modules.title: Corporate Strategy
modules.objectives: Explain diversification strategies and when they create vs destroy value; analyze vertical integration decisions; evaluate M&A rationale; apply portfolio analysis frameworks (BCG matrix).
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — corporate-level strategy, portfolio choices, and growth actions
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson and teacher-reviewed examples for this topic.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — corporate-level strategy, portfolio choices, and growth actions — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Evaluate three included growth choices for Northstar: acquire a battery-recycling shop for $600,000; open its own retail stores for $900,000; or buy a 30% stake in an unrelated meal-delivery app for $500,000. Northstar can invest at most $700,000, has repair expertise but no retail-property team, and currently sends used batteries to outside recyclers. Recommend one feasible choice or reject all. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: corporate-strategy classification, relatedness, vertical-integration direction, synergy, capability fit, execution risk, and financing feasibility for each choice. Evaluation: correct strategy classification (40%), use of supplied financial and capability facts (40%), and disciplined recommendation (20%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion with included facts and cited course rules.

modules.title: Strategy Execution
modules.objectives: Translate strategy into actionable plans using OKRs and the Balanced Scorecard; identify common execution failures; design accountability structures that connect daily work to strategic goals.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — implementation plans and strategic alignment
modules.videoNote: John Doerr TED talk — “Why the secret to success is setting the right goals,” an OKR-focused execution supplement
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — implementation plans and strategic alignment — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Translate Northstar’s goal—raise service retention from 78% to 88% while reducing average repair time from 5 days to 3 within two quarters—into an execution system. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: two qualitative Objectives, three measurable Key Results per Objective, one Balanced Scorecard measure and target for each perspective, named owners, review cadence, and one early-warning trigger. Evaluation: measurable alignment (45%), ownership and monitoring design (35%), and professional clarity (20%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion or method with cited case facts, calculations, or course rules.

modules.title: Writing the Strategic Plan
modules.objectives: Structure a complete strategic plan document; write a compelling executive summary; draft strategic objectives and initiatives; include a high-level financial projections overview.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — strategic, tactical, and operational plans
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson and teacher-reviewed examples for this topic.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Principles of Management — strategic, tactical, and operational plans — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Draft a two-page strategic plan for Northstar using only the supplied course case and a planning assumption of $1.2 million annual revenue with a maximum $250,000 first-year investment. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: an executive summary, situation analysis, three objectives, two initiatives per objective, owners, milestones, a financial range with explicit assumptions, and one stop condition. Evaluation: internal consistency (40%), evidence and assumptions (35%), and decision-ready structure (25%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion or method with cited case facts, calculations, or course rules.

modules.title: The Business Case
modules.objectives: Explain the purpose and structure of a business case; build a financial justification using ROI and payback period; conduct a risk analysis; write a clear recommendation section.
modules.readingNote: OpenStax Introduction to Business 2e — decision-ready business planning and financial assumptions
modules.videoNote: GIIS Learn Portal — use the module lesson and teacher-reviewed examples for this topic.
modules.practiceNote: OpenStax Introduction to Business 2e — decision-ready business planning and financial assumptions — concept checks and application practice
modules.assignment: Prepare a business case for Northstar to buy diagnostic software costing $80,000 upfront plus $10,000 per full operating year. Implementation takes three months; fees and benefits begin only at go-live. After go-live, expected annual labor savings are $35,000 and avoided rework is $15,000. Use a three-year operating horizon after go-live and do not discount cash flows. Submit: one clearly labeled document or slide deck. Include: problem and alternatives, benefit/cost table, three-year net benefit, ROI using total cost, payback measured from project start, a 3×3 risk matrix with three risks, and a clear approve/reject recommendation. Evaluation: accurate calculations (40%), risk and alternative analysis (35%), and concise recommendation (25%). Evidence requirement: justify each conclusion with included facts, calculations, and cited course rules.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the difference between strategy and tactics?
options: Strategy is short-term; tactics are long-term
Strategy sets the overall direction and goals; tactics are the specific actions taken to achieve them
Strategy is developed by frontline employees; tactics are set by executives
Strategy and tactics mean the same thing in business
questions.answer: Strategy sets the overall direction and goals; tactics are the specific actions taken to achieve them
questions.explanation: Strategy answers 'where do we want to go and why?'; tactics answer 'how do we get there?' Strategy is long-term and directional; tactics are short-term and operational.

questions.question: In the PESTLE framework, what does the 'L' stand for?
options: Logistics
Leadership
Legal
Labor
questions.answer: Legal
questions.explanation: PESTLE stands for Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental. Legal factors include regulations, employment law, consumer protection, and industry-specific compliance.

questions.question: Porter's Five Forces framework is used primarily to:
options: Analyze a company's internal strengths and weaknesses
Assess industry attractiveness and competitive intensity
Plan the organizational structure of a firm
Determine a company's marketing budget
questions.answer: Assess industry attractiveness and competitive intensity
questions.explanation: Porter's Five Forces examines: threat of new entrants, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers, threat of substitutes, and competitive rivalry — all of which determine how attractive and profitable an industry is.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: The resource-based view of the firm argues that competitive advantage comes from:
options: Possessing valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable resources
A plan that defines goals and how to achieve them over the long term
Internal capabilities and resources the company does exceptionally well
The sequence of activities that create value for the customer and generate profit
questions.answer: Possessing valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable resources
questions.explanation: The best answer is Possessing valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable resources.

questions.question: A company pursuing a differentiation strategy aims to:
options: Produce goods at the lowest possible cost and pass savings to customers
Offer products or services perceived as unique and worth a premium price
Serve only a narrow customer segment at the lowest cost
Avoid competing with other firms entirely
questions.answer: Offer products or services perceived as unique and worth a premium price
questions.explanation: Differentiation strategy creates value by offering something distinct — quality, brand, features, design — that allows the firm to charge a premium. The goal is perceived uniqueness, not just low cost.

questions.question: Which statement best describes strategic intent?
options: A list of this week’s tasks
An ambitious long-term direction that focuses and stretches the organization
A completed annual budget
A legal requirement for public companies
questions.answer: An ambitious long-term direction that focuses and stretches the organization
questions.explanation: Strategic intent expresses a sustained direction and aspiration that coordinates choices beyond short-term operational tasks.

questions.question: Which decision is made at the functional strategy level?
options: Whether to enter healthcare
Whether a business unit competes through differentiation
How marketing will allocate channels to support the chosen positioning
Whether to acquire an unrelated company
questions.answer: How marketing will allocate channels to support the chosen positioning
questions.explanation: Functional strategy translates higher-level direction into choices for areas such as marketing, operations, finance, or human resources.

questions.question: A new privacy law changes how a firm may use customer data. In PESTLE, this is primarily a:
options: Technological factor
Legal factor
Environmental factor
Supplier-power factor
questions.answer: Legal factor
questions.explanation: A binding privacy rule belongs in the legal category, although it may also create technological and operational consequences.

questions.question: When conducting a SWOT analysis, which two categories relate to the external environment?
options: Strengths and Weaknesses
Opportunities and Threats
Strengths and Opportunities
Weaknesses and Threats
questions.answer: Opportunities and Threats
questions.explanation: In SWOT: Strengths and Weaknesses are internal factors the organization controls. Opportunities and Threats are external forces from the market, competition, and macro-environment.

questions.question: Blue Ocean Strategy encourages companies to:
options: Compete more aggressively in existing markets
Create uncontested market space and make the competition irrelevant
Copy best practices from industry leaders
Reduce costs by eliminating all premium features
questions.answer: Create uncontested market space and make the competition irrelevant
questions.explanation: Blue Ocean Strategy (Kim & Mauborgne) focuses on creating new demand in an uncontested market space ('blue ocean') rather than competing in saturated 'red oceans' where rivalry drives down profits.

questions.question: Under the resource-based view, which resource is most likely to support sustained advantage?
options: A commonly available office suite
A valuable, rare capability that is difficult to imitate and supported by the organization
A temporary price discount
A public industry report available to all rivals
questions.answer: A valuable, rare capability that is difficult to imitate and supported by the organization
questions.explanation: The VRIO logic connects value, rarity, imitability, and organizational support to the possibility of sustained competitive advantage.

questions.question: Which activity is part of a firm’s primary value chain rather than a support activity?
options: Human-resource management
Technology development
Inbound logistics
Firm infrastructure
questions.answer: Inbound logistics
questions.explanation: Inbound logistics is a primary activity directly involved in receiving and handling inputs; HR, technology, and infrastructure support the chain.

questions.question: A focused differentiation strategy is most appropriate when a firm:
options: Serves a narrow segment with distinct needs and can offer valued uniqueness
Must be the lowest-cost producer in every segment
Owns businesses in unrelated industries
Avoids choosing a target customer
questions.answer: Serves a narrow segment with distinct needs and can offer valued uniqueness
questions.explanation: Focused differentiation targets a specific segment and builds features or service that the segment values enough to support the position.

questions.question: A scooter-rental market has modest startup costs, several established operators competing for riders and city contracts, and customers who compare prices in an app. Which pair of Porter's Five Forces is most directly supported by these facts?
options: Threat of new entrants and competitive rivalry
Supplier power and threat of substitutes
Buyer power and supplier power
Threat of substitutes and supplier power
questions.answer: Threat of new entrants and competitive rivalry
questions.explanation: Modest startup costs support a threat of new entrants, while several established operators competing for riders and contracts support strong rivalry.

questions.question: A SWOT lists “strong repair expertise” and “new city subsidies.” Which classification is correct, and why?
options: Repair expertise is an internal strength; city subsidies are an external opportunity
Repair expertise is an external opportunity; city subsidies are an internal strength
Both are internal strengths because both may improve performance
Both are external opportunities because management can choose to use them
questions.answer: Repair expertise is an internal strength; city subsidies are an external opportunity
questions.explanation: SWOT treats the organization’s capability as internal and the city policy as an external condition.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Strategic intent, as defined by Hamel and Prahalad, refers to:
options: An ambitious long-term aspiration that stretches the organization beyond current resources
A company's annual profit target
A plan that defines goals and how to achieve them over the long term
Internal capabilities and resources the company does exceptionally well
questions.answer: An ambitious long-term aspiration that stretches the organization beyond current resources
questions.explanation: The best answer is An ambitious long-term aspiration that stretches the organization beyond current resources.

questions.question: Which PESTLE factor would include a government's decision to raise the corporate tax rate?
options: Social
Technological
Environmental
Political
questions.answer: Political
questions.explanation: Government policy decisions — including tax rates, trade tariffs, subsidies, and regulatory changes — fall under the Political factor of PESTLE analysis.

questions.question: High bargaining power of suppliers in Porter's Five Forces typically leads to:
options: Lower input costs for companies in the industry
Reduced profitability for companies in the industry
Easier entry for new competitors
Higher customer satisfaction
questions.answer: Reduced profitability for companies in the industry
questions.explanation: When suppliers have high bargaining power, they can raise prices or reduce quality, squeezing the margins of companies that depend on them. This reduces industry profitability.

questions.question: A company's value chain consists of:
options: The sequence of activities that create value for the customer and generate profit
The stock market valuation of the company over time
The list of investors who own shares in the company
The company's pricing structure from wholesale to retail
questions.answer: The sequence of activities that create value for the customer and generate profit
questions.explanation: Porter's value chain maps primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing & sales, service) and support activities (infrastructure, HR, technology, procurement) that collectively create value.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Cost leadership strategy is most effective when:
options: Price-sensitive customers make purchase decisions primarily on cost
Cost Leadership, Differentiation, and Focus
Produce goods at the lowest possible cost and pass savings to customers
Leadership
questions.answer: Price-sensitive customers make purchase decisions primarily on cost
questions.explanation: The best answer is Price-sensitive customers make purchase decisions primarily on cost.

questions.question: Unrelated diversification means a company expands into:
options: A new geographic market with the same product
An industry with no significant strategic fit with its current businesses
The same industry with a slightly modified product
A supplier's business in its existing industry
questions.answer: An industry with no significant strategic fit with its current businesses
questions.explanation: Unrelated (conglomerate) diversification involves entering industries unrelated to current operations. It may spread risk but often fails to create value because there are no synergies between businesses.

questions.question: A Key Result in an OKR framework must be:
options: Qualitative and inspirational
Specific and measurable with a defined target
Approved by the board of directors
Set only at the company level, not team level
questions.answer: Specific and measurable with a defined target
questions.explanation: Key Results are quantitative measures of progress toward an Objective. They must include a specific metric and target (e.g. 'Increase NPS from 42 to 60 by Q4') so progress can be objectively assessed.

questions.question: The executive summary of a strategic plan should:
options: Include every detail from all sections of the plan
Be written first and provide a detailed financial model
Concisely capture the most critical points so busy readers can grasp the plan quickly
Only be read by the finance team
questions.answer: Concisely capture the most critical points so busy readers can grasp the plan quickly
questions.explanation: An executive summary is a distilled version of the full plan — usually 1–2 pages — that enables executives and board members to understand the strategy without reading every section. It is written last but placed first.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: In a business case, a risk matrix typically evaluates each identified risk by:
options: Likelihood and impact
Its financial cost alone
Strategy and tactics mean the same thing in business
Adapts products and strategies to fit each local market
questions.answer: Likelihood and impact
questions.explanation: The best answer is Likelihood and impact. It connects the correct answer to Business Strategy & Writing final concepts and separates it from plausible distractors.

questions.question: A merger creates value only if the combined firm can realize benefits that exceed:
options: The acquisition premium and integration costs
The target’s employee count
The number of competitors
The length of the press release
questions.answer: The acquisition premium and integration costs
questions.explanation: Synergy must be large and achievable enough to exceed the price premium, integration expense, execution risk, and value available without the deal.

questions.question: Which sentence is most appropriate in a decision-ready strategic plan?
options: We will probably grow a lot soon
Increase renewal from 70% to 82% by Q4; the customer lead owns monthly progress reviews
Everyone should try harder
Success will be obvious when it happens
questions.answer: Increase renewal from 70% to 82% by Q4; the customer lead owns monthly progress reviews
questions.explanation: Decision-ready writing names a measurable outcome, deadline, accountable owner, and review mechanism instead of relying on vague aspiration.

questions.question: An execution plan has ambitious targets but no owners or review cadence. Its central weakness is:
options: Too much market data
Missing accountability and feedback loops
Excessive legal protection
Too many financial calculations
questions.answer: Missing accountability and feedback loops
questions.explanation: Execution requires named responsibility, timing, measures, and review routines that reveal problems early enough for corrective action.

questions.question: A high-growth, low-share business in a BCG-style portfolio is commonly called a:
options: Cash cow
Question mark
Mature core
Divested liability
questions.answer: Question mark
questions.explanation: A low-share unit in a high-growth market may require substantial investment and a deliberate decision to build, partner, harvest, or exit.

questions.question: Which Balanced Scorecard measure belongs most clearly to the internal-process perspective?
options: Return on invested capital
Customer referral rate
Order-error rate
Employee certification completion
questions.answer: Order-error rate
questions.explanation: Order-error rate measures the reliability of an internal operating process; the other choices align more closely with financial, customer, or learning perspectives.

questions.question: A Balanced Scorecard adds which perspective to financial, customer, and internal-process measures?
options: Learning and growth
Competitor pricing only
Quarterly revenue only
Legal ownership structure
questions.answer: Learning and growth
questions.explanation: The four standard Balanced Scorecard perspectives are financial, customer, internal processes, and learning and growth.

questions.question: A strategic analysis capstone project should demonstrate all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Integration of external and internal analysis
Clear strategic recommendations with rationale
Memorization of the textbook's exact definitions
Evidence-based reasoning supported by real sources
questions.answer: Memorization of the textbook's exact definitions
questions.explanation: A strategic analysis tests analytical thinking, synthesis, and judgment — not memorization. Strong capstone work integrates frameworks, applies them to real data, and makes reasoned recommendations.

questions.question: Choose the best answer: Which of the following is the best example of a 'Star' in the BCG Matrix?
options: A product with high market share in a high-growth market
A legacy product with stable sales in a stagnant market
A new geographic market with the same product
Low market growth and high relative market share
questions.answer: A product with high market share in a high-growth market
questions.explanation: The best answer is A product with high market share in a high-growth market.

questions.question: The Balanced Scorecard's Financial Perspective typically measures:
options: Customer satisfaction scores and Net Promoter Score
Revenue, profit margins, return on investment, and economic value added
Number of training hours and employee retention rates
Process cycle time and defect rates
questions.answer: Revenue, profit margins, return on investment, and economic value added
questions.explanation: The Financial Perspective tracks traditional accounting measures: revenue growth, profitability, ROI, and EVA — answering 'How do we look to shareholders?'

questions.question: A project costs $120,000 and is expected to produce $50,000 annual net cash benefit for three years. Without discounting, calculate payback period and ROI using total benefit.
options: Payback is 2.4 years and three-year ROI is 25%
Payback is 1.6 years and three-year ROI is 20%
Payback is 2.4 years and three-year ROI is 125%
Payback is 3 years and three-year ROI is 30%
questions.answer: Payback is 2.4 years and three-year ROI is 25%

questions.question: A software project costs $80,000 upfront and $10,000 annually, saves $50,000 annually, begins operating immediately, and is evaluated over three years without discounting. Which recommendation correctly states the financial case and addresses a high-likelihood migration risk?
options: Approve a staged pilot: total cost is $110,000, total benefit is $150,000, net benefit is $40,000, ROI is about 36%, and stop if validated migration accuracy misses the agreed threshold
Approve immediately: total cost is $80,000, ROI is 88%, and migration accuracy need not be tested
Reject because total benefit is $150,000 and total cost is $110,000, producing a $40,000 loss
Delay indefinitely because a high-likelihood risk makes calculation and mitigation irrelevant
questions.answer: Approve a staged pilot: total cost is $110,000, total benefit is $150,000, net benefit is $40,000, ROI is about 36%, and stop if validated migration accuracy misses the agreed threshold
questions.explanation: Over three years, cost is $80,000 + 3($10,000) = $110,000 and benefit is 3($50,000) = $150,000. Net benefit is $40,000 and ROI is $40,000 ÷ $110,000 ≈ 36%; a staged pilot and measurable stop threshold address migration risk.

quizQuestions.question: Strategy is best defined as:
options: A detailed daily task list
A plan that defines goals and how to achieve them over the long term
A budget forecast for the next quarter
An employee performance review system
quizQuestions.answer: A plan that defines goals and how to achieve them over the long term
quizQuestions.explanation: Strategy defines where an organization wants to go and the choices it makes to get there — it is directional, long-term, and involves trade-offs.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an example of a tactical decision?
options: Deciding to expand into the Asian market
Choosing which social media platform to advertise on this month
Setting a 5-year revenue growth target
Acquiring a competitor company
quizQuestions.answer: Choosing which social media platform to advertise on this month
quizQuestions.explanation: Tactics are specific, short-term actions that implement strategy. Choosing a social media platform for this month's campaign is tactical; the strategic decision would be 'we will grow brand awareness in the 18–24 demographic.'

quizQuestions.question: Which choice is a business-level strategy rather than a corporate- or functional-level choice?
options: Enter an unrelated industry
Compete in the current market through focused differentiation
Change the payroll approval workflow
Acquire a supplier in another country
quizQuestions.answer: Compete in the current market through focused differentiation
quizQuestions.explanation: Business-level strategy defines how a business competes in a product market; corporate strategy chooses businesses, while functional choices support execution.

quizQuestions.question: In PESTLE analysis, rising inflation and interest rates would be classified under:
options: Political
Economic
Social
Technological
quizQuestions.answer: Economic
quizQuestions.explanation: Inflation, interest rates, exchange rates, unemployment, and GDP growth are all Economic factors in the PESTLE framework.

quizQuestions.question: Porter's Five Forces that specifically examines the threat from completely different types of products or services is:
options: Competitive rivalry
Threat of new entrants
Threat of substitutes
Bargaining power of buyers
quizQuestions.answer: Threat of substitutes
quizQuestions.explanation: Threat of substitutes measures the risk that customers will switch to alternative products that fulfill the same need — e.g., streaming services as a substitute for movie theaters.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following would INCREASE the threat of new entrants in an industry?
options: High capital requirements to enter the market
Strong customer loyalty to existing brands
Low economies of scale advantages
Strict government licensing requirements
quizQuestions.answer: Low economies of scale advantages
quizQuestions.explanation: When incumbents have no significant scale advantages, new entrants can compete on equal footing from a smaller size, making entry easier. High barriers (capital, loyalty, licensing) reduce entry threat.

quizQuestions.question: Buyer power is likely strongest when:
options: Customers face high switching costs and few alternatives
Customers can compare many similar offers and switch at low cost
Suppliers are concentrated
Entry requires large irreversible investment
quizQuestions.answer: Customers can compare many similar offers and switch at low cost
quizQuestions.explanation: Many alternatives, price transparency, and low switching costs let buyers pressure firms on price, quality, and terms.

quizQuestions.question: In a SWOT analysis, 'Strengths' refers to:
options: External market conditions favoring the company
Internal capabilities and resources the company does exceptionally well
Competitive threats from rival firms
Regulatory gaps the company can exploit
quizQuestions.answer: Internal capabilities and resources the company does exceptionally well
quizQuestions.explanation: Strengths are internal positive attributes — brand reputation, proprietary technology, skilled workforce, strong cash flow, or superior processes — that give the company an advantage.

quizQuestions.question: Core competencies, according to Prahalad and Hamel, must satisfy which criteria?
options: They must be easy to imitate so competitors can benchmark them
They must provide potential access to a wide variety of markets, contribute to customer benefits, and be difficult for competitors to imitate
They must be focused exclusively on cost reduction
They must be owned by only one department within the firm
quizQuestions.answer: They must provide potential access to a wide variety of markets, contribute to customer benefits, and be difficult for competitors to imitate
quizQuestions.explanation: Prahalad & Hamel's three tests for a core competency: (1) provides access to multiple markets, (2) makes a significant contribution to customer value, and (3) is difficult to imitate.

quizQuestions.question: Porter's value chain divides company activities into primary activities and support activities. Which of the following is a PRIMARY activity?
options: Human resource management
Firm infrastructure
Inbound logistics
Technology development
quizQuestions.answer: Inbound logistics
quizQuestions.explanation: Primary activities in Porter's value chain are: Inbound Logistics, Operations, Outbound Logistics, Marketing & Sales, and Service. Support activities (HR, infrastructure, technology, procurement) enable the primary activities.

quizQuestions.question: Porter's three generic strategies are:
options: Growth, Stability, and Retrenchment
Cost Leadership, Differentiation, and Focus
Market Penetration, Development, and Diversification
Innovation, Imitation, and Cost Cutting
quizQuestions.answer: Cost Leadership, Differentiation, and Focus
quizQuestions.explanation: Porter's Generic Strategies: Cost Leadership (compete on lowest cost), Differentiation (compete on uniqueness/premium), and Focus (serve a narrow segment with either cost or differentiation).

quizQuestions.question: A company 'stuck in the middle' in Porter's framework refers to a firm that:
options: Operates in the middle market segment geographically
Has not committed to any one generic strategy and therefore achieves mediocre performance
Generates average returns consistent with industry norms
Pursues a focused differentiation strategy effectively
quizQuestions.answer: Has not committed to any one generic strategy and therefore achieves mediocre performance
quizQuestions.explanation: Porter warned that firms trying to be 'all things to all customers' — pursuing both low cost and differentiation without focus — end up stuck in the middle: not the cheapest, not the most differentiated, with poor profitability.

quizQuestions.question: Blue Ocean Strategy's 'Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create' grid helps companies:
options: Manage employee performance reviews
Redesign their value proposition by questioning all industry assumptions
Calculate their cost of goods sold
Plan their quarterly marketing budget
quizQuestions.answer: Redesign their value proposition by questioning all industry assumptions
quizQuestions.explanation: The ERRC grid forces companies to decide: what factors to eliminate (industry assumptions), reduce (below standard), raise (above standard), and create (new, never before offered) — reconstructing value in an uncontested space.

quizQuestions.question: A firm redesigns its value chain to deliver acceptable quality at the industry’s lowest sustainable cost. Which strategy is it pursuing?
options: Cost leadership
Unrelated diversification
Product development only
Backward integration
quizQuestions.answer: Cost leadership
quizQuestions.explanation: Cost leadership requires a value-chain system that lowers cost while maintaining the level of value target customers expect.

quizQuestions.question: Related diversification occurs when a company expands into:
options: Businesses that share strategic fit with existing operations
Any industry with high growth potential regardless of connection
International markets for the first time
A joint venture with a direct competitor
quizQuestions.answer: Businesses that share strategic fit with existing operations
quizQuestions.explanation: Related diversification leverages shared capabilities, customers, technology, or distribution channels. Strategic fit allows synergies that can lower costs or increase revenue beyond what either business could achieve alone.

quizQuestions.question: Backward vertical integration means a company:
options: Moves into distributing and selling its products directly to consumers
Acquires or develops control over its input suppliers
Exits the market and outsources all production
Diversifies into an unrelated industry
quizQuestions.answer: Acquires or develops control over its input suppliers
quizQuestions.explanation: Backward integration moves 'upstream' in the supply chain toward raw materials or component suppliers. Forward integration moves 'downstream' toward distribution or retail.

quizQuestions.question: A manufacturer acquires one of its direct competitors. This is best classified as:
options: Backward vertical integration
Forward vertical integration
Horizontal integration
Unrelated diversification
quizQuestions.answer: Horizontal integration
quizQuestions.explanation: Buying a competitor at the same stage of the value chain is horizontal integration and may increase scale, market share, or consolidation risk.

quizQuestions.question: In a BCG-style portfolio, a business with high relative share in a slow-growth market is commonly classified as a:
options: Star
Question mark
Cash cow
New entrant
quizQuestions.answer: Cash cow
quizQuestions.explanation: A high-share unit in a mature, slow-growth market is expected to generate cash that can support other priorities, subject to the model’s limits.

quizQuestions.question: The most common reason strategies fail at the execution stage is:
options: The strategy was too innovative
Poor alignment between strategy and day-to-day operations, incentives, and accountability
Executives spent too much time planning
The strategy targeted too profitable a market
quizQuestions.answer: Poor alignment between strategy and day-to-day operations, incentives, and accountability
quizQuestions.explanation: Research shows 60–90% of strategies fail in execution. The most common causes: employees don't understand the strategy, incentives don't align with it, and no one is accountable for results.

quizQuestions.question: The Balanced Scorecard's four perspectives are:
options: Planning, Organizing, Leading, Controlling
Financial, Customer, Internal Process, Learning & Growth
Revenue, Costs, Assets, Equity
Vision, Mission, Values, Goals
quizQuestions.answer: Financial, Customer, Internal Process, Learning & Growth
quizQuestions.explanation: Kaplan & Norton's Balanced Scorecard balances financial measures with operational drivers: Financial (shareholder view), Customer (customer experience), Internal Process (operational efficiency), and Learning & Growth (capability building).

quizQuestions.question: In Strategy Execution, An OKR Objective should be:
options: Numerical and expressed as a percentage
Qualitative, inspirational, and describe the desired outcome
Limited to the finance department
Set quarterly by the board of directors
quizQuestions.answer: Qualitative, inspirational, and describe the desired outcome
quizQuestions.explanation: In the OKR framework, the Objective is the qualitative, motivating description of what you want to achieve ('Become the most loved brand in our category'). The Key Results are the quantitative measures of success.

quizQuestions.question: Which is the strongest Key Result for an Objective to improve customer onboarding?
options: Create a world-class experience
Work harder on onboarding
Raise 30-day activation from 62% to 75% by quarter end
Meet regularly about customers
quizQuestions.answer: Raise 30-day activation from 62% to 75% by quarter end
quizQuestions.explanation: A Key Result should be measurable and time-bound so the team can determine whether the desired outcome actually changed.

quizQuestions.question: The correct order of sections in a well-structured strategic plan is typically:
options: Financial projections → Executive Summary → Objectives → Initiatives
Executive Summary → Situation Analysis → Strategic Objectives → Initiatives → Financials
Initiatives → Objectives → Financial Projections → Executive Summary
Mission Statement → Tactics → Budget → Executive Summary
quizQuestions.answer: Executive Summary → Situation Analysis → Strategic Objectives → Initiatives → Financials
quizQuestions.explanation: A strategic plan flows logically: executive summary (overview) → situation analysis (where we are) → strategic objectives (where we want to go) → initiatives (how we'll get there) → financial projections (what it will cost and return).

quizQuestions.question: How should the length of a strategic plan’s executive summary be determined?
options: Use exactly one page for every plan
Match the document scale and audience while keeping the decision, rationale, value, and main risks concise
Repeat every section word for word
Omit the recommendation until the final appendix
quizQuestions.answer: Match the document scale and audience while keeping the decision, rationale, value, and main risks concise
quizQuestions.explanation: An executive summary should be proportionate to the plan and reader, giving decision-makers the recommendation and essential evidence without duplicating the full document.

quizQuestions.question: Which strategic objective is most decision-ready?
options: Improve the company soon
Increase recurring-service revenue from $2.0M to $2.6M by December while maintaining gross margin above 40%
Become the best business
Launch several useful initiatives
quizQuestions.answer: Increase recurring-service revenue from $2.0M to $2.6M by December while maintaining gross margin above 40%
quizQuestions.explanation: A decision-ready objective defines the outcome, baseline, target, deadline, and a guardrail against damaging tradeoffs.

quizQuestions.question: The primary purpose of a business case document is to:
options: Provide a detailed history of the company's past decisions
Persuade decision-makers to approve a specific investment or course of action
Replace the annual strategic plan
Satisfy external audit requirements
quizQuestions.answer: Persuade decision-makers to approve a specific investment or course of action
quizQuestions.explanation: A business case is a persuasive document that justifies why a particular investment or decision should be made, using evidence: problem analysis, solution options, financial justification, risk assessment, and a clear recommendation.

quizQuestions.question: Payback period in a business case refers to:
options: The time required for an investment to generate enough returns to recover its initial cost
The interest rate on a company's debt
The number of months until a new hire becomes fully productive
The penalty for breaking a supplier contract early
quizQuestions.answer: The time required for an investment to generate enough returns to recover its initial cost
quizQuestions.explanation: Payback period = Initial Investment / Annual Net Cash Flow. It answers: 'How long until we get our money back?' Shorter payback periods indicate lower risk.

quizQuestions.question: In a risk matrix, a risk with HIGH likelihood and HIGH impact should be:
options: Accepted without a mitigation plan
Ignored since all risks eventually resolve themselves
Prioritized for immediate mitigation planning
Disclosed only to external auditors
quizQuestions.answer: Prioritized for immediate mitigation planning
quizQuestions.explanation: High-likelihood, high-impact risks represent the greatest threats to a project or investment. They require active mitigation strategies, contingency plans, and close monitoring.

quizQuestions.question: An initiative costs $100,000 and produces $130,000 in total measured benefit. Using ROI = (benefit − cost) / cost, what is ROI?
quizQuestions.explanation: Net benefit is $30,000; dividing by the $100,000 cost gives 0.30, or 30 percent ROI.
